articles.text:
There has scarcely been a public question since the war broke out, that has been given such attention or the discussion of which has been characterized with more bitter feeling than the question of the manufacture of oleomargarine. The prime difficulty has been that in all legislation and attempted legislation on the subject, each side claims that it is entirely right and the opposition is entirely wrong. A conference of the leading men on both sides should be able to formulate legislation that will be at least fairly satisfactory to all concerned. Such a conference never has been held and it is doubtful if it ever will be. The chief points brought against oleomargarine are that it is a fraud to sell it as butter, that it is driving pure buttery out of the market and that it is unhealthy. The first point is undoubtedly the best one and all fair-minded people will agree that oleomargarine should be sold under its true name. The market does not show any decrease in price on good butter for several years and oleomargarine really only comes into competition with the poorer grades of butter. That it is unhealthy is as yet unproved, except in cases where diseased animals have been used; these being cases for health officers to rule upon. The oleomargarine people should be willing to sell their product under its true name, and in this way we believe that nine-tenths of the discussion would be stopped. We do not, however, see the justice of putting a tax on the manufacture of oleomargarine. If it is sold under its true name and the consumer knows what he is buying, it would be as sensible to put a tax on any newly-discovered, low-priced article that comes into competion with a high-priced article. For instance, if it is right to tax oleomargarine, manufactured and sold under its true name, it would be right to tax the telephone up to a point where they must charge the same as the telegraph. There is certainly competition, but competition drives monopoly to the wall and lessens prices to consumers. We hope the only national legislation to be passed on the subject will be to compel oleomargarine to be sold under its true name.

(Yesterday's Bismarck Tribune brought the news that the oleomargarine bill had passed the Senate with amendmen[ts?] reducing the tak from five to two cents per pound. To become a law, it must be approved now by the House and President.
articles.summary: Editorial argues oleomargarine should be sold under its true name but not taxed; notes the Senate passed the oleomargarine bill with the tax cut to two cents.

articles.headline: Commissioners' Meeting.
articles.text:
The board of county commissioners met in special session the afternoon of July 20.

Present: Truscott, McKenzie, Goodall and Clerk Williamson.

Jorgens & Rider's liquor bond presented and accepted.

The Bad Lands Cow Boy presented bills for printing, one for $10.75, one for $31.00 and one for $1.50. Allowed, and a warrant for the amount, $43.25 drawn in payment.

On motion, the board adjourned to meet on the morning of the 21st., at nine o'clock.

J. C. Williamson, County Clerk.

MEETING ON MORNING OF JULY 21.

R. Robert's attorney presented his lease of building for county purposes, which was signed and filed.

The county clerk presented a bill for services rendered for and in behalf of W. F. Van Driesche, Talleyrand Martin, as judges and C. F. Ellison as clerk of an election held in Medora for the purpose of organization of school township number 1. Allowed, and warrants drawn for the amounts.

On motion, the board adjourned to meet at half past twelve.

MEETING IN AFTERNOON OF JULY 21.

The board met at 12:30.

Meeting called to order by the chairman of the board.

Present: Commissioners Truscott, McKenzie and Goodall and Clerk Williamson.

The commissioners proceeded to divide the county of Billings into Commissioners districts as follows:

Commissioner's District No. 1.

Beginning at a point where the line between town 144 and 145 north intersect the boundary line between the territories of Dakota and Montana, thence south along said boundary line to the line between towns 140 and 141 north thence east along said town line to the line between ranges 101 and 102 west thence north along said range line to the line between towns 144 and 145 north thence west along said town line to the place of beginning.

Commissioner's District No. 2.

Beginning at a point where the line between towns 140 and 141 north intersect the boundary line between the territories of Dakota and Montana thence south along said boundary line to the line between 136 and 137 north thence east along said town line between ranges 101 and 102 west thence north along said range line to the line between towns 140 and 141 west thence west along said town line to the place of beginning.

Commissioner's District No. 3.

Beginning at a point where the line between 136 and 137 north intersect the boundary line between the territories of Dakota and Montana thence south along said boundary line to the line between towns 132 and 133 north thence east along said town line to the line between ranges 101 and 102 west thence north along said range line to the line between towns 136 and 137 north thence along said town line to the place of beginning.

On motion a resolution was adopted setting forth that at this annual election in November, that district No. 1 should elect a commissioner for the period of one (1) year and that district No. 2 should elect one [commissioner?] for the period of two (2) years and that district No. 3 should elect one commissioner for the period of three (3) years.

The petitions of jurors for their fees in Justice's court in the case of Ferris and Merrifield vs. Mrs. Malloy presented to the board and the same were laid over till their next meeting.

Justice Copeland's quarterly report submitted for examination and not being satisfactory, was laid over also.

On motion, Dan. McKenzie was appointed a committee of one to procure and arrange necessary furniture of the court house.

On motion the board adjourned.

J. C. Williamson, County Clerk.
articles.summary: Minutes of the Billings County commissioners' meetings of July 20 and 21, 1886: liquor bond, printing bills, courthouse lease, school township election, division of the county into three commissioner districts, and a jurors' fee petition in Ferris and Merrifield vs. Mrs. Malloy.

articles.text: Talking of roping, by the way, a cowboy by the name of Henry Williams, in the employ of the Neimmella cattle company on the Little Missouri, accomplished a feat on Wednesday last with a grass rope which heads the record. He was hunting saddle horses, and had come across two or three head of the missing animals drinking at the river. He rode down to turn them out, when a full-grown wild goose flew up from under a bunch of undergrowth on the bank of the river and passed straight in front of him. He had his rope uncoiled and ready for use with which to secure the horses out of the river, and quick as thought as the bird flew past him he pitched the rope at it and succeeded in catching it by one wing. He took the bird home to the ranch and it will be kept and tamed if possible. So far, nothing with four feet has been considered safe from being ensnared by the treacherous lariat, but a bird on the fly, even though as big as a wild goose, has hitherto been considered safe from any such mode of capture. The man who accomplished the above is well known as one of the most skilled ropers in the Little Missouri country, and to those who have witnessed him swing the lariat the feat does not seem so surprising.—[Stockgrowers' Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted from the Stockgrowers' Journal: Neimmela cowboy Henry Williams roped a flying wild goose on the Little Missouri.

articles.text: The above article makes a pair with the feat of Jess. Reeves in catching a jack rabbit with a [lariat?] published in the Cow Boy, t[he f]irst of June. Either seems imposible until one sees what an expert can do with a rope.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy pairs the goose-roping story with Jess Reeves's roping of a jack rabbit reported June 1.

articles.headline: Alfalfa Feeding.
articles.text:
The demand for beef is growing more rapidly than the herds are increasing. In the year 1860 there were 814 cattle in the United States for every 1,000 of our population. To-day there are only 775 head of cattle to each 1,000 of population, a very considerable falling off in the relative supply, notwithstanding that during this period the whole of Montana, Dakota, Idaho, eastern Oregon, Nevada, Wyoming, Colorado, Arizona, most of New Mexico and nearly one-half of Texas have been withdrawn from the domination of the Indian and filled to overflowing with cattle. The increase in these states and territories alone, since 1860, has been over 15,000,000 head of cattle. Still, with this wonderful extension of the business into new fields, and the saving of every she animal of the bovine race for breeding purposes, the increase of population has been so rapid and continuous that we have not been able to keep up our beef supply. No one will for a moment dispute the statement that the population of this country will go on increasing at a proportionate rate, and that in consequence in the year 1910 we will have 100,000,000 people to eat beef. Where is this supply to come from? There is no more unoccupied country. As a general proposition [the?] country is full of cattle. With our [population?] doubled the demand for beef will be doubled. How can this demand be met? Only by producing double the amount of beef on the same ground now occupied. This condition can only be reached in a small area of the country, for the reason that the larger per cent. of the arid region, or permanent range country, has no adequate water supply and no greater number of cattle can be raised than can gain their subsistence from the range in its present condition. Then it is a safe and reasonable conclusion that year by year the beef supply will grow less per capita, and that there will be a gradual advance in prices in proportion as the supply is short.

If then, there is no danger of an over-supply, and a consequent lowering of prices, as a business proposition it is safe to spend money in the development of a country where increased supplies may be had, so long as you keep those expenditures at a point below which you can secure a present return. The future will guard itself.

There is yet another advantage. By the production of hay the ranchman is put in virtual control of the market. The beef market of the east has for years been regulated by Chicago. The vast numbers of grass Texans thrown upon that market in July and August lower prices from one to two cents a pound. During the two and a half months following the great runs of northwestern beef from the ranges still further reduce prices. But all range beef must go to the market, for they cannot be held on the open range. In consequence the shipper must take such a price as he is offered. But with great stacks of alfalfa in the fields the fat steers may be held over until the demand creates satisfactory prices.

A fat three-year-old steer, weighing 1,100 pounds off the range in October, may be put in an open lot anywhere on the valley lands, and fed hay through the winter with an absolute certainty of gaining 200 pounds gross, and a probability of seventy-five pounds more if judiciously handled. It is always profitable to feed a beef steer if he is thriving and "doing well," as feeders say, provided the feed is secured at a reasonable price. He is laying on fat that has a commercial value greater than the raw material that was converted into fat.

To back up this alfalfa feeding idea the writer has taken great pains to secure facts and figures, some of which are herewith presented. Two years ago a gentleman living near Ogden, Utah, fed a bunch of steers for several months, weighing the hay fed out each day and the steers every week. The result showed that 2,240 pounds of alfalfa put on an even hundred pounds of flesh or growth. Another gentleman living fifteen miles from Salt Lake City brought fifteen three-year-old steers out of pasture seven miles distant, drove them to his pens and weighed them, paying therefore at so much a pound. They were weighed on the first day of November. On the 31st of December they were sold to a Salt Lake butcher, driven fifteen miles to the slaughter-house and weighed, having again been purchased at so much a pound. They had gained 120 pounds, or two pounds a day, and during the time had been fed nothing but alfalfa hay in an open lot.—[Nevada Letter Cheyenne Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted Nevada letter from the Cheyenne Journal arguing that alfalfa feeding lets ranchmen hold fat steers and profit from a growing beef demand.

articles.text: T. Martin is the weather prophet of this country and justly so as he has a tri-daily report of the weather extending back many years. A comparison of the first half of July with other periods shows that there has never been known such a warm spell as the first sixteen days of July. For all that time, the weather averaged 102 degrees in the shade and 114 in [the sun?] between six in the morning and six in the evening.
articles.summary: T. Martin's weather records show the first 16 days of July were the hottest on record.

articles.text: In view of the approaching legislative convention, it especially behooves the citizens of Billings Co. to inquire who is the best man to represent their interests at Bismarck. With the right kind of an effort it might be possible to secure a man from Stark county to represent the west Missouri country, who appreciated the needs of legislation for the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Editorial urges Billings County to seek a legislative candidate who understands Bad Lands needs.

articles.text: The present drought has brought out a number of experiences, encouraging to stockmen. There has only been one year in Montana that compared with this for dryness and that was early in the '70's. There was almost no rain until the middle of September. Then the ground received several good soakings and there has not been better grass, except in size of the blades, before or since.
articles.summary: Comment that a comparable Montana drought in the 1870s was followed by excellent grass.

articles.text: The butchers of New York have decided to boycott the N. P. Ref. Car Co's. retail shops there. It is supposed that the first effect of this was [seen?] in some broken windows in one of the shops, a few days ago. We cannot see how a boycott against the shops will be effective, as the whole business, from beginning to end is in the hands of the Co., and it would be a difficult thing to boycott the customers of thirty or more different stores.
articles.summary: New York butchers boycott the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co.'s retail shops.

articles.text: The Territorial Republican convention for the purpose of putting in nomination a candidate for delegate to congress, will be held in Yankton, Wednesday, September 22, 1886. Except for the fact that there are more carpet-bag politicions to the square inch in Dakota than any other part of this fair land and that every mother's son of them is scheming for office, Delegate Gifford stands the best chance of securing the plum. The outcome, in any event, is wrapped in a more impenetrable obscurity than the result of the deliberation of a coroner's jury.
articles.summary: The Territorial Republican convention will meet at Yankton September 22; Delegate Gifford is favored.

articles.text: In spite of the large numbers of horses that have been brought to the Little Missouri ranges the last three years, the price holds up better than in almost any other part of the range country. This is probably explained by the facts that there is a constantly growing demand among the farmers east of us for work horses and that the horse ranches on the river have taken all the good mares that have been brought in. In any event, the price of good horses is as high as it was three years ago and there seems no immediate prospect of there being any break in the market. Within three years, however, the horse ranches here will be able to supply a large demand for first-class heavy work horses as well as the best quality of cow-horses.
articles.summary: Horse prices on the Little Missouri hold up despite heavy imports of horses.
